lessons.title: The Metrics That Matter: Traction, Unit Economics and Burn

children.text: A founder opens her deck with "we crossed 5 lakh app downloads". The investor writes nothing down. She follows with "38% of customers who bought in January bought again within 90 days, and we make ₹606 of contribution on an average order". Now he is taking notes. Downloads are a number. Repeat rates and contribution margins are a business. This lesson teaches you the metrics investors actually price, how to calculate each one, and which numbers to stop putting on slides.

body.text: Three questions sit behind every metric an investor asks for. Do people want it, does each customer make more than they cost, and how long can you survive while proving both? Traction, unit economics and burn. Everything else is decoration.

children.text: Traction: Which Numbers Belong to Your Model
There is no universal traction metric. A SaaS investor and a lending investor want completely different numbers, and using the wrong set signals that you do not understand your own business.

body.caption: The metrics investors ask for, by business model

cells: Orders per month, average order value, repeat purchase rate
Return to origin rate on cash-on-delivery orders
Monthly and annual recurring revenue, net revenue retention, logo churn
Gross merchandise value, take rate, net revenue, buyer repeat rate
Supply-side churn: sellers who stop listing
Daily and monthly active users, day-30 retention, revenue per user
The ratio of daily to monthly actives
Disbursals, assets under management, net interest margin
Collection efficiency and credit cost as the book seasons
Revenue per employee, which shows whether it scales

body.title: Vanity numbers vs numbers investors price

columns.label: Vanity
points: Gross merchandise value quoted as revenue
Social media followers and press coverage
Total addressable market from a consultant's report
Cumulative totals since inception, which can only go up

columns.label: What gets priced
points: Paying customers this month, and how many came back
Net revenue after discounts, returns and platform fees
A bottom-up market built from real customer counts and prices
Month-on-month growth, contribution margin and burn multiple

body.text: The most common mistake in Indian marketplace decks is quoting gross merchandise value as if it were revenue. If ₹50 crore of goods move through your platform at an 8% take rate, your revenue is ₹4 crore, not ₹50 crore. Investors will find this in the first diligence call, and it costs you credibility on everything else in the deck.

body.title: GMV is not revenue
body.prompt: A Surat textile marketplace processes ₹50 crore of orders in a year and keeps an 8% commission. What is its net revenue, in ₹ crore?
body.explanation: ₹50 crore × 8% = ₹4 crore. Gross merchandise value measures activity on the platform. Revenue is only the slice the platform keeps, and the gap between them is where inflated pitches live.

children.text: Retention: The Metric That Cannot Be Faked

markDefs.definition: A group of customers who first bought or signed up in the same month, tracked over time so you can see how many keep coming back.

children.text: Growth can be bought. Retention cannot. That is why investors ask for
cohort

data: take everyone who first bought in January, and track what share of them are still active each month afterwards. The shape of that curve decides whether your marketing spend is building an asset or filling a leaking bucket.

body.title: Two retention curves from the same January cohort (% still active)

series.label: Curve that flattens: a real product
Curve that keeps falling: a leaking bucket

body.text: Investors look for the flattening, not the starting height. A curve that settles at 38% means roughly four in ten customers have made this a habit, and every rupee of marketing adds to a growing base. A curve still falling at month 6 means you are renting customers, and growth stops the day you stop spending.

children.text: In subscription businesses the same idea is measured in rupees rather than people, through net revenue retention. It asks what happened to last year's revenue from last year's customers, after upgrades, downgrades and cancellations.

body.caption: Net revenue retention, measured on the same set of customers a year apart

children.text: A Bengaluru SaaS company starts the year with ₹100 lakh of recurring revenue from existing customers. They upgrade by ₹18 lakh, downgrade by ₹4 lakh and cancel ₹6 lakh. NRR is (100 + 18 − 4 − 6) ÷ 100 = 108%. Above 100% means the existing base grows even if you never sign a new customer, which is the single most attractive number in Indian SaaS fundraising.
Unit Economics: Does One Customer Make Money?

Unit economics strips the company down to one customer. Ignore salaries, office rent and the founder's laptop for a moment, and ask a single question: when one more customer buys, does the company end up with more cash or less? Three formulas answer it.

body.latex: \text{CAC} = \frac{\text{Sales and marketing spend in a period}}{\text{New customers acquired in that period}}
body.caption: Customer acquisition cost. Include agency fees, discounts and sales salaries, not just ad spend.
What one order leaves behind before any fixed costs
Lifetime value on a contribution basis, and the ratio investors test it against

children.text: Worked Example: Nolo Naturals
Nolo Naturals is an illustrative Jaipur skincare brand selling on its own website and on marketplaces. Its average order value is ₹1,200. Here is what one order actually leaves behind.

Now the acquisition side. Nolo spent ₹6 lakh on performance marketing last month and got 500 first-time customers, so CAC is ₹6,00,000 ÷ 500 = ₹1,200. On the first order the company earns ₹606 and spent ₹1,200 to get it, a loss of ₹594. Every D2C brand in India looks like this at first order. The business only works if customers come back.

stats.label: At 2.5 lifetime orders
stats.context: Below the 3 times benchmark: too thin to scale

body.text: Notice what fixes this business, and what does not. Raising ₹20 crore changes nothing about a 1.26 ratio, it just funds the same loss at a larger scale. Getting the fourth repeat order, lifting average order value with bundles, or cutting RTO losses by pushing prepaid orders: those change the ratio. This is exactly why investors ask for unit economics before they ask for projections.

children.text: Using revenue instead of contribution.

Nolo's LTV on a revenue basis at 2.5 orders is ₹3,000, which looks like a healthy 2.5 times CAC. On a contribution basis it is ₹1,515. Only the second number is real, because the rest went to suppliers and couriers.
Assuming a lifetime nobody has lived yet.
A company 14 months old cannot claim a three-year customer life. Investors will ask for the cohort data behind the assumption, and if the oldest cohort is 9 months old, that is the evidence you have.
Leaving costs out of CAC.

Discounts, influencer payments, agency retainers, marketplace commissions and the salaries of the people running growth all belong in CAC. Counting only the advertising spend can halve the number and tells the investor more about your rigour than about your business.

body.title: How long until a customer pays for themselves?
body.prompt: A SaaS company charges ₹5,000 a month, earns 80% gross margin on that revenue, and spends ₹48,000 to acquire one customer. How many months of subscription does it take to recover the acquisition cost?
body.explanation: Monthly contribution is ₹5,000 × 80% = ₹4,000. CAC payback is ₹48,000 ÷ ₹4,000 = 12 months. Anything beyond about 12 months means the company funds a year of customer costs upfront, which forces it to keep raising just to grow.

children.text: Burn: How Efficiently Do You Convert Cash Into Growth?

Lesson 1.1 covered net burn and runway. Investors go one step further and ask what the burn bought. The burn multiple compares cash consumed against new recurring revenue created, and it has become a standard question in Indian rounds since the funding market tightened in 2022.

body.latex: \text{Burn multiple} = \frac{\text{Net cash burned in a period}}{\text{Net new ARR added in that period}}
body.caption: Rupees burned for every rupee of new recurring revenue. Lower is better.
Reading the burn multiple (a widely used rule of thumb, not a standard)

cells: Under ₹1 burned per ₹1 of new recurring revenue
Exceptional efficiency, a strong Series A case
Acceptable if growth is very fast
Hard to raise without a clear fix

body.label: The post-2022 shift in India
body.value: Efficiency questions now come before growth questions
body.context: In the 2021 funding boom, growth at any burn was rewarded. After the correction, Indian investors ask about contribution margin, burn multiple and the path to profitability in the first meeting, not the fourth.

body.title: Which slide gets the second meeting?
body.question: Four founders each lead with one headline. Which one will an investor take most seriously?
options: "12 lakh app downloads and 4 lakh registered users"
"₹210 crore of GMV run rate on our platform"
"₹1.8 crore ARR, growing 14% month on month for 7 months, with net revenue retention of 112%"
"Featured in three national publications and a ₹1.2 lakh crore addressable market"
body.explanation: Only the third option contains revenue that is real, a growth rate that is sustained, and evidence that existing customers expand rather than leave. Downloads, GMV run rates, press coverage and market size reports are all numbers that can be true while the business is not working.

body.title: Two D2C brands, one term sheet
body.scenario:
Both brands did ₹9 crore of revenue last year and want ₹15 crore.
Brand X: average order value ₹1,600, contribution margin 22%, CAC ₹1,900, 1.8 orders per customer on average, 70% of orders are cash on delivery with a 24% return to origin rate, and growth is entirely from paid ads.
Brand Y: average order value ₹950, contribution margin 41%, CAC ₹700, 3.4 orders per customer, 62% prepaid orders, and 45% of monthly revenue comes from customers acquired more than six months ago.
body.prompt: Which brand raises more easily, and what are the two most important fixes for the other?
body.modelAnswer:
Brand Y raises more easily.
Run the numbers. Brand Y: contribution per order is ₹950 × 41% = ₹389.50, so LTV is ₹389.50 × 3.4 = ₹1,324, against CAC of ₹700. That is a ratio of about 1.9, and repeat customers already fund nearly half of monthly revenue.
Brand X: contribution per order is ₹1,600 × 22% = ₹352, so LTV is ₹352 × 1.8 = ₹633.60, against CAC of ₹1,900. The ratio is about 0.33, meaning every customer acquired destroys roughly ₹1,266 of value. Scale makes that worse, not better.
The two fixes for Brand X, in order:
1. Fix the RTO problem. A 24% return rate on 70% cash-on-delivery orders means roughly one order in six is shipped twice and sold zero times. Push prepaid with discounts, add address verification and confirmation calls, and stop advertising in pin codes with the worst return history.
2. Fix repeat purchase. At 1.8 orders per customer, the brand is renting customers from an ad platform. Until repeat rates rise, more funding just buys the same loss at a bigger scale.
A careful investor would tell Brand X to come back in two quarters with a better ratio, not a bigger revenue number.

body.title: The ratio investors test
body.textWithBlank: Most investors want lifetime value to be at least ___ times customer acquisition cost, measured on contribution and not on revenue.
body.explanation: Three times is the common working benchmark. It leaves room for fixed costs, failed experiments and the reality that early customer lifetime estimates are usually optimistic.

body.title: The metrics pack investors will ask you for
steps: Monthly revenue for the last 18 months, split into new and repeat.
A cohort table showing what each month's customers did in every month since.
CAC by channel, with every cost included, not just ad spend.
Contribution margin per unit, built up line by line from price to net.
Monthly net burn, closing cash and runway, month by month.
Customer concentration: revenue share of your top five customers.
For SaaS, net revenue retention and logo churn. For D2C, RTO and repeat rate. For lending, collection efficiency.

cards.definition: All sales and marketing spend in a period divided by the new customers acquired in that period.
What one sale leaves after the direct costs of delivering it: goods, fulfilment, payment fees and returns.
Contribution per order multiplied by expected lifetime orders. Measured on contribution, never on revenue.
Acquisition cost divided by monthly contribution: how many months until a customer repays what they cost.
Last year's revenue from last year's customers after upgrades, downgrades and cancellations, as a percentage.
Net cash burned divided by net new recurring revenue added. Lower means growth is bought more efficiently.
Return to origin: a shipped order the customer refuses or fails to accept, common in cash-on-delivery e-commerce in India.
The share of transaction value a marketplace keeps as revenue, the bridge between GMV and real revenue.

points: Use the traction metrics that belong to your model. The wrong set signals that you do not understand your own business.
GMV, downloads and registered users are activity, not revenue. Investors price paying customers and net revenue.
Retention cannot be bought. A cohort curve that flattens proves a habit, and one that keeps falling proves you are renting customers.
Contribution margin is price minus all direct costs. Nolo Naturals keeps ₹606 of a ₹1,200 order, which is the only money available to cover CAC.
Measure LTV on contribution, not revenue, and target at least 3 times CAC. A ₹1,200 CAC against ₹1,515 of lifetime contribution does not scale.
CAC payback of about 12 months or less keeps a company from having to raise simply to keep growing.
The burn multiple asks what your burn bought. Since 2022, Indian investors ask about efficiency in the first meeting, not the fourth.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment, legal or financial advice. Benchmarks such as 3 times LTV to CAC, 12-month payback and burn multiple bands are widely used rules of thumb that vary by sector and market conditions, not standards. Nolo Naturals, Brands X and Y and the other figures are illustrative. Speak to a qualified professional before making funding decisions for your company.
